extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, federal judges, law clerks, and parties in patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Determine whether asserted patent claims are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using the Alice/Mayo two-step framework and applicable Rule 12(c) pleading standards in district-court litigation. Includes when such questions can be resolved on the pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12(c) standard for judgment on the pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruling on a Rule 12(c) motion the court must accept as true all well-pleaded allegations in the non-movant’s pleadings and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-movant; judgment under Rule 12(c) is appropriate only where 'the movant clearly establishes that no material issue of fact remains to be resolved and that [the movant] is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For patent §101 motions, eligibility can be resolved on the pleadings when there are no factual allegations that, when taken as true, prevent deciding the eligibility question as a matter of law (see Data Engine Techs. LLC v. Google). Courts should therefore examine whether factual disputes (e.g., about whether claim features are conventional) preclude resolution at the pleadings stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory scope of patentable subject matter (35 U.S.C. § 101) and enumerated exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 permits patents for any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (or improvements thereof). The Supreme Court recognizes three exceptions: laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that are directed to any one of these three categories are 'directed to' ineligible subject matter and must be tested under the Alice/Mayo framework; these exceptions are considered basic tools beyond patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts use a two-step framework: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea); (2) if so, search for an 'inventive concept' that transforms the ineligible concept into 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If at step one the claims are not directed to an ineligible concept, the inquiry ends and §101 is satisfied; if directed to an ineligible concept, the court proceeds to step two to determine whether the claim elements (alone or in combination) supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step One — consider claims in their entirety and focus on claimed advance
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one, 'the claims are considered in their entirety to ascertain whether their character as a whole is directed to excluded subject matter' — the inquiry looks to the 'focus of the claimed advance over the prior art' to determine what the claim is really directed to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must be careful not to oversimplify the claims or describe them at an improperly high level of abstraction; it is insufficient to merely identify a patent-ineligible concept underlying the claim — the court must determine whether that concept is what the claim is 'directed to' (see Enfish, McRO, Rapid Litigation Management).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step Two — inventive concept inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two the court examines claim elements and their combination to determine whether they transform the ineligible concept into something 'significantly more' — i.e., whether there is an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than a patent on the ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept requires more than performance of 'well-understood, routine, [and] conventional activities previously known to the industry.' An inventive concept can arise from a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces. Whether elements (or their combination) are well-understood, routine, or conventional is a question of fact (Berkheimer) and may preclude resolution at the pleadings stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative precedent analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts often compare the claims at issue to claims considered in the body of §101 decisions to determine whether they are analogous to previously held eligible or ineligible claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the most analogous Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Enfish, McRO, Interval Licensing, Amdocs) and explain similarities and differences in focus, claimed advance, and claim detail; overreliance on superficial similarities may mischaracterize claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness requirement for 'exemplary' or 'representative' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party argues that one or a few claims are 'exemplary' or 'representative' of a larger set, the party must show how those claims are actually representative of other independent and dependent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusive or conclusory assertions that claims are representative are typically insufficient; however, if the parties agree that a claim is representative, the court may accept that agreement. A movant should identify where in the briefing each challenged claim is addressed and how the representative claim covers others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating claims as mere results — look for specific steps achieving the result
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'recite more than a mere result' — i.e., that 'recite specific steps . . . that accomplish the desired result' — are less likely to be treated as directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the claim language provides concrete steps, structures, or limitations that accomplish the asserted technological improvement (e.g., synchronous and secure updating between processes in Mach-derived systems) rather than merely reciting the end result or high-level goal (citing Finjan).

rubrics_metrics.name: If claims are not directed to an abstract idea at Step One, do not reach Step Two
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court concludes at step one that claims are not directed to an abstract idea (or other ineligible concept), the §101 inquiry ends and the court need not proceed to step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a common procedural shortcut endorsed by Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Core Wireless) — ensure the step-one analysis is thorough before invoking this conclusion.
